text.content:
• What a domain is: any power with people working for it: a noble house, a temple, a thieves' guild, a druid circle, a dragon and its servants. A domain run by the player characters is an organisation. One run by the GM is a realm.
  • Intrigue: when two domains set out to destroy each other, that is an intrigue. It runs alongside ordinary adventuring and ends in a showdown: the heroes against the enemy's leader and lieutenants, their armies in battle (Chapter 4), or both.
  • How a domain falls: only when its leader is beaten, whether killed, captured, banished or brought to surrender. Its followers may gather under someone new, but that is a new realm.
  • Optional rules. Like strongholds, domains are for tables that want them.

• When: the moment the party holds a stronghold (Chapter 1) and has followers (Chapter 2). A Seat counts as a stronghold.
  • Officers: every player character is an officer. A lieutenant (Chapter 2) can act for the domain but is not an officer.
  • The army: the units your strongholds and follower tables have raised (Chapters 1 and 3). They answer to the officers, and each officer commands as many units as Chapter 4 allows.
  • Choose a type: one of the eight organisation types below. It sets the starting skills and defences, a domain power, a domain feature and a special unit.
  • Development points: spend 8 at founding, and 8 more each time the domain's size grows. Each point raises one skill by 1 (+4 at most) or one defence score by 1 (18 at most). Players take turns spending them.

• Size: 1 to 5. A new organisation is size 1. Size measures reach, not acreage: a size 3 domain might hold a county, or a few streets of a great city.
  • Skills: four modifiers, from −1 to +4.
    • Diplomacy: alliances, favours, borrowed troops.
    • Espionage: spies, secrets, sabotage.
    • Lore: research, magic, old knowledge.
    • Operations: mustering, building, supply, and anything else.
  • Defences: three scores, from 10 to 18. An enemy's test against a defence must reach its score.
    • Communications: how fast and safely orders travel.
    • Resolve: how much the domain's people believe in it.
    • Resources: money, stores, gear, and whatever else the domain hoards.
  • Defence levels: each defence also has a level from −3 to +3, which starts at 0 when an intrigue begins (Defence levels, below).

  • Growing: a domain grows by 1 size each time it defeats another domain, to 5 at most. At size 5 the GM may still award 8 development points for each domain defeated.

• The roll: d20 + the domain skill's modifier against a DC: Easy 10, Moderate 12, Hard 15 or Severe 20. Against an enemy defence, the DC is that defence's score.
  • An officer's skill: once per intrigue, an officer who has a matching skill rolls the test with Advantage.
Domain skillMatching skills
DiplomacyEtiquette, Heraldry, Gather Information
EspionageStealth, Disguise, Reading Lips
LoreAncient History, Spellcraft, Religion, Astrology
OperationsEngineering, Endurance, Survival, Animal Handling
  • Outside an intrigue: an officer gives orders and the domain's people carry them out over days or weeks. About one domain test a week is right, or one per session if your table doesn't track the days. The GM sets the DC and what success means.
  • What starts an intrigue: asking around, reading old histories and talking to the enemy's neighbours does not. Spying on a villain, sabotaging them or turning their allies does: the GM calls the intrigue.
  • Lore is no shortcut: agents can fetch what would be easy but slow for the heroes to get. Anything dangerous or difficult, the heroes do themselves.

• One villain: an intrigue is between the heroes' organisation and one realm. A campaign with lieutenants who answer to a greater villain can run one intrigue for each.
  • Turns: each side takes turns equal to 4 + its size.
  • How a turn works:
  • The GM picks the realm's action in secret.
  • The players name their organisation's action and which officer leads it.
  • The GM reveals the realm's action, both sides roll, and the results are shared.
  • Who knows what: spies on both sides see most of what happens. The exceptions are musters and changes to a domain's skills or defences. The other side learns that something happened, but finding out what takes Espionage.
  • The bigger domain: if one side has more turns, it takes the extra ones at the start if it began the intrigue, or at the end if it didn't.
  • Pacing: the GM decides how often a turn comes round: one a week, one a day, one after each fight, or two whenever experience is awarded. The last turn usually comes just before the showdown.
  • After the intrigue: defence levels drift one step back towards 0 each week.

Domain actions

On each turn the domain takes one domain action. The usual ones:

  • Raise a defence: a test with any skill that fits how you go about it, against Moderate 12 + the defence's current level. Success raises it one level; a natural 20 raises it two.
  • Lower an enemy defence: a test with a skill that fits, against that defence's score. Success lowers it one level; a natural 20 lowers it two.
  • Spy: an Espionage test against the enemy's Communications. On a success, learn one of: its defence scores, its defence levels, its skills, its army, or something else the GM allows.
  • Borrow a unit: a Diplomacy test to have an NPC realm lend its special unit for the next battle. The DC follows the realm's attitude: Hostile 20, Suspicious 15, Neutral 12, Friendly 10, Allied no test. Each realm lends one unit an intrigue, so ask before the enemy does. Fail by 5 or more and its attitude worsens one step.
  • Muster: raise or hire one unit (Chapter 4), paying its first season's upkeep. No test is needed unless the GM thinks it could fail. The unit answers to the officer who mustered it.
  • Upgrade: improve the gear of the units one officer commands, at Chapter 4's prices.
  • Fortify: an Operations test to build on ground you hold: Moderate 12 for a wall or ditch, Hard 15 for a tower. Succeed by 5 or more and it stands at the end of this turn; succeed by less and it stands at the end of the next; fail by 4 or less and it takes three turns; fail by 5 or more and you can try again next turn. Outside an intrigue, read each turn as a week.
  • Muster the special unit: see your organisation type. Once per intrigue, the unit fights one battle and then leaves. It costs no upkeep but counts towards its commander's units.
  • A feature: your organisation type's domain feature.
  • Anything else the players can describe and the GM agrees to.

Bonuses add up as a level rises, so a +3 has the +1 and +2 effects as well; penalties add up the same way as it falls.

• Each officer has one, sized by the domain (d4 at size 1 to d12 at size 5). Realm leaders and lieutenants have them too.
  • Rolling: at the start of any fight against officers of the opposed domain, each officer may roll their die and add it to the domain's pool. An officer may hold theirs back for a harder fight. Once rolled, an officer's die can't be rolled again until they finish an Extended Rest (Chapter 1).
  • Spending: any officer can take dice from the pool to fuel the domain's power, in the way the power says. Dice left unspent at the end of the fight are lost.

• Taxes: each season, a stronghold that holds land (a keep, tower, temple, grove or castle) collects taxes, tithes or tribute from its demesne. They pay the upkeep of the units that stronghold and its follower rolls gave you (Chapters 1 and 3), with 100 gp × stronghold level to spare.
  • What they don't pay for: mercenaries and units mustered in an intrigue. A bigger army is paid from treasure, plunder and allies.
  • Lean seasons: a demesne that was raided or besieged that season, or whose domain ends the season at Resources level −2 or worse, pays half. Units left short go unpaid (Chapter 4). A demesne in enemy hands pays its new master.
  • Raids and plunder: a season camped on someone's demesne takes 500 gp × their domain size; winning a battle against a town or stronghold plunders 1,000 gp × their domain size. Either way, its lord now has a grudge, and very likely an intrigue.
  • No taxes: an establishment earns its own income instead (Chapter 1). A barbarian camp lives on its raids, and a pirate ship on its plunder.

• The showdown: the heroes fight the enemy leader and lieutenants as an ordinary fight, while the armies fight a battle around them (Heroes in battle, Chapter 4).
  • Victory: beat the leader and the realm falls. The heroes' organisation grows by 1 size and gains 8 development points. Its strongholds can be taken as a grant (Chapter 1), with their demesnes.
  • Defeat: an organisation whose officers are all beaten falls in the same way. Survivors can found a new one.

Each type gives starting skills and defences, a domain power, a domain feature and a special unit. Officers spend power dice on their own turn, as part of their action, unless the power says otherwise.

Adventuring Company

Delvers, sellswords and troubleshooters who never quite settled down. In Arneyan: the Wayfinders, the Keepers of Tariel, the Eltor Free Company, Moon's Free Company.

  • Skills: Diplomacy −1, Espionage +0, Lore +1, Operations +2.
  • Defences: Communications 11, Resolve 12, Resources 10.
  • Power, Long Odds: after a creature rolls a save against something you did, spend a die: it rerolls and keeps the lower result.
  • Feature, Call in a Favour: once per intrigue, borrowing a realm's special unit takes no turn.
  • Special unit, the Free Company: Moderate Operations test. Veteran light infantry, Size 1d6. Delvers: ignores ground, and has Advantage on Attack against monster units.

Martial Order

A regiment, a city watch or a company of knights, drilled and proud of it. In Arneyan: the Knights of Holfast, the Eltor Cavalry Guard, the Boldock Wall-Knights, the Wardens of the Wilds.

  • Skills: Diplomacy +1, Espionage +0, Lore −1, Operations +2.
  • Defences: Communications 12, Resolve 11, Resources 10.
  • Power, Cut Them Down: once per round, out of turn, when a creature you can see moves within your reach or range, spend any number of dice: make one weapon attack against it with Advantage, adding the dice to its damage.
  • Feature, Drilled: once per intrigue, a Hard Operations test. On a success, your Resolve level can't fall below 0 for the rest of the intrigue.
  • Special unit, the Old Guard: Moderate Operations test. Elite heavy infantry, Size 1d6. Steady: can't be moved against its will, and its Brace succeeds without a roll.

Merchant House

A trading company, a guild or a family of bankers. Money talks, and they own the language. In Arneyan: the Merchant Houses of Lankhmar, the Merchant's Guild.

  • Skills: Diplomacy +1, Espionage +0, Lore −1, Operations +2.
  • Defences: Communications 11, Resolve 10, Resources 12.
  • Power, Money Well Spent: when you miss with an attack, spend a die to reroll it once. When you hit, you can instead spend a die to add twice its number to the damage.
  • Feature, No Expense Spared: once per intrigue, as a battle begins, pay 100 gp × your domain's size and make a Hard Operations test. On a success, two of your defences rise one level.
  • Special unit, Sellswords of Renown: Moderate Operations test. Veteran heavy infantry, Size 1d8. Paid to Stay: Advantage on Morale checks.

Arcane Circle

A college of mages, a secret cabal or a tower of scholars. In Arneyan: O.M.G.A. (the Opal Mages Guild Association), the Scholars of the Silver Tower, the Sorcerers' Cabal.

  • Skills: Diplomacy +0, Espionage +1, Lore +2, Operations −1.
  • Defences: Communications 12, Resolve 10, Resources 11.
  • Power, Wellspring: as your action, spend a die: regain one spent spell slot of a level no higher than the die shows (5th at most). Or, when you hit with a weapon, spend a die: the hit deals twice the die's number more as acid, cold, fire or lightning damage.
  • Feature, Unpick the Weave: once per intrigue, a Lore test against the enemy's Communications. On a success, learn the spells of one enemy officer, and your officers have Advantage on saves against that officer's spells until the intrigue ends.
  • Special unit, the Iron Ranks: Moderate Lore test. Regular heavy infantry of constructs, Size 1d8. Mindless and Spell-Wise (Chapter 4).

Wild Pact

A druid circle, a hunters' lodge or a people sworn to the land. In Arneyan: the Natural Order, the Tanatharen Circle.

  • Skills: Diplomacy +1, Espionage +0, Lore +2, Operations −1.
  • Defences: Communications 10, Resolve 12, Resources 11.
  • Power, Grasping Thorns: as your action, spend a die: a creature you can see within 30ft makes a Reflex save against your Class Save DC (or Spell Save DC) or is Restrained for rounds equal to the die. It can tear free with a Hard Strength or Tumbling check as its action, taking 1d10 piercing per domain size.
  • Feature, The Land Rises: once per intrigue, a Lore test against the enemy's Resources. On a success, its Resources level falls two steps.
  • Special unit, the Great Toad: Hard Lore test. A monster unit (Chapter 4) of one huge beast: Level 10, Size 1d8, Damage 2. Gulp: a successful Power roll deals 1 more casualty.

Noble House

A lord and their court, ruling land and people by right of blood or law. In Arneyan: House Talithaln, House Yisen.

  • Skills: Diplomacy +2, Espionage +0, Lore −1, Operations +1.
  • Defences: Communications 10, Resolve 12, Resources 11.
  • Power, Blood Will Tell: spend a die: choose one attribute; for rounds equal to the die, you have Advantage on checks and saves that use it.
  • Feature, Old Friendships: once per intrigue, a unit you borrow from a realm comes with its Size die one step larger.
  • Special unit, the Household Knights: Moderate Operations test. Veteran heavy cavalry, Size 1d6. Lance Charge: its first attack in a battle has Advantage.

Holy Order

A church, a monastery or a crusading order, and sometimes a cult. In Arneyan: the Order of Tyr, the Order of Eilistraee.

  • Skills: Diplomacy +0, Espionage −1, Lore +2, Operations +1.
  • Defences: Communications 11, Resolve 12, Resources 10.
  • Power, Answered Prayer: as your action, spend a die: a servitor from your god's row (The Temple, Chapter 1) arrives, of a Type up to half the die (round up). It acts on your turn and stays 1 + domain size rounds. Like any servitor it never uses solo rules, and it doesn't count as your one spell-made attacker.
  • Feature, Blessing of Arms: once per intrigue, a Hard Lore test. On a success, one unit you control has Advantage on Attack and on Morale checks until the end of its next battle.
  • Special unit, the Sworn Crusaders: Hard Diplomacy test. Veteran medium infantry, Size 1d6, Radiant (Chapter 4). At the end of the next deployment, one enemy green or regular unit's Size die shrinks a step (1d4 at least).

Thieves' Guild

An underworld syndicate, a spy network or a smugglers' ring. In Arneyan: the Guild in Opal, the Guild of Lankhmar.

  • Skills: Diplomacy +0, Espionage +2, Lore −1, Operations +1.
  • Defences: Communications 12, Resolve 10, Resources 11.
  • Power, Find the Gap: spend a die: until the end of your next turn, attacks against one creature you can see have Advantage, and the first hit against it deals extra damage equal to the die.
  • Feature, Plans within Plans: once per intrigue, an Espionage test against the enemy's Communications. On a success, your Communications level rises one step and theirs falls one.
  • Special unit, the Cutthroats: Moderate Operations test. Elite light infantry, Size 1d6, Morale 2 lower. Dirty Fighters: Advantage on Attack against diminished units.

Building a villain's realm

  • Type: an organisation type above, or a realm type below.
  • Size: usually within 1 of the heroes' organisation.
  • Development points: 8 × its size, spent like the players'.
  • Officers: a leader and lieutenants from Monsters & Treasure. They have power dice. A realm type uses the domain power of whichever organisation type suits it best.
  • Stronghold: where its leader lives and keeps its treasure, with the villain powers of Chapter 3.

Building an NPC realm

  • The essentials: a type, a leader's name and manner, a size, a stronghold, and its attitude to the heroes: Hostile, Suspicious, Neutral, Friendly or Allied. It can have another type's special unit if that fits.
  • Hostile is not villainous: a hostile realm has old grudges, but it isn't trying to destroy the heroes. Only a villain's realm takes part in an intrigue. Other realms lend units or stay out.

Realm types

Skills are Diplomacy, Espionage, Lore and Operations; defences are Communications, Resolve and Resources. A monster unit uses Chapter 4's Monsters as units, with the creature from Monsters & Treasure. Arneyan examples are in brackets. No devil rules openly in Arneyan: an infernal court is mortals bound by infernal contract, or a rakshasa's underworld.
